title: From IITs to India's nuclear programme: How Nehru shaped modern Indian science
content_html:
Nehru regarded science and technology as powerful instruments of economic and social transformation. (X/INCIndia)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Jawaharlal Nehru’s engagement with science began long before he entered politics. At Trinity College, Cambridge, he studied geology, chemistry and botany, completing the Natural Science Tripos with a second-class honours degree. Although politics came to dominate his life, his interest in science endured.

In his words: “Though I have long been a slave driven in the chariot of Indian politics… my mind has often wandered to the days when, as a student I haunted the laboratories of that home of science, Cambridge…. In later years, through devious processes, I arrived again at science, when I realised that science was of the very texture of life…. Politics led me to economics, and this led me inevitably to science and the scientific approach to all our problems and to life itself. It is science alone that could solve these problems of hunger and poverty.”

In an essay in the collection Science and Technology in India (1977), G H Keswani went a step further, speculating on the career Nehru might have pursued had he remained in science: “We may ask a somewhat fanciful question. If Jawaharlal had continued with his career in science, it is probable that he would have become a notable experimental scientist. Indeed, he was an Experimentalist.”

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

On Nehru’s birth anniversary (November 14), we look at how his faith in science shaped India’s scientific institutions and policies after Independence.

Before Independence: The foundations of Indian science

“It can scarcely be denied that scientific research in India was already quite robust before Independence,” writes Keswani. Scientists such as Jagadish Chandra Bose, C V Raman, K S Krishnan, Meghnad Saha, P C Mahalanobis, D S Kothari, Birbal Sahni and Homi J Bhabha belonged to this pre-Independence generation.

As one account notes, experimental research did not always require expensive equipment, and individual ingenuity could lead to breakthroughs even in the absence of substantial government patronage. 

Also Read | ‘True revolutionary’: Why Bhagat Singh chose Jawaharlal Nehru over Subhas Bose

The idea of placing science at the centre of India’s development had also begun to take shape before Independence. In 1938, the Congress established the National Planning Committee under Jawaharlal Nehru, during the presidency of Subhas Chandra Bose. The committee sought to envision India’s economic and industrial future, drawing on the expertise of scientists, industrialists and economists. Among those associated with it were scientists Meghnad Saha and J C Ghosh, and industrialists Purshottamdas Thakurdas, Walchand Hirachand and Ambalal Sarabhai.

Story continues below this ad

The outbreak of World War II in 1939 and the launch of the Quit India Movement in 1942 disrupted the committee’s work. However, many of its members remained committed to the cause of scientific, technological and industrial development in the years that followed. Nehru had articulated his own faith in science even earlier. In 1937, he declared: “The future belongs to science and those who make friends with science and seek its help for the advancement of humanity.”

How Nehru built India’s scientific infrastructure

“Nehru’s consistent support for science as the first prime minister of India, as we shall see, enabled science institutions to thrive,” notes author Indira Chowdhury in Growing the Tree of Science: Homi Bhabha and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (2016).

Atomic research particularly interested Nehru. Homi J Bhabha, who had established the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in 1945 with support from the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust, became a central figure in shaping India’s nuclear programme. Working closely with Nehru, Bhabha helped build the institutional foundations of an indigenous atomic energy programme. The Atomic Energy Commission was established on August 10, 1948. In 1954, a separate Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) was created under the direct charge of the Prime Minister, with Bhabha as its secretary.

Also Read | How Nehru saw India: The modernist rooted in its civilisational legacy

Alongside atomic research, Nehru championed the expansion of scientific and technical education. The Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), modelled partly on the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), were established over the course of the 1950s and early 1960s, beginning with IIT Kharagpur in 1951. Their objective was to develop highly skilled scientists and technologists who could contribute to research, design and development and help India achieve technological self-reliance.

Story continues below this ad
Nehru, with Bhabha, inaugurating the atomic reactor Apsara in 1957. (Nehru Archive)

Nehru also sought to establish a broader policy framework for scientific advancement. On March 4, 1958, Parliament adopted the Scientific Policy Resolution, which articulated the government’s commitment to using science and technology for national development and public welfare.

The resolution stated: “The key to national prosperity, apart from the spirit of the people, lies, in the modern age, in the effective combination of three factors, technology, raw materials and capital, of which the first is perhaps the most important, since the creation and adoption of new scientific techniques can, in fact, make up for a deficiency in natural resources, and reduce the demands on capital. But technology can only grow out of the study of science and its applications…”

Nehru at the Central Scientific Research Institute in Hyderabad in 1952. (Nehru Archive)

In 1962, Nehru constituted the Indian Parliamentary and Scientific Committee to encourage greater parliamentary engagement with science. Lal Bahadur Shastri was its first chairman.

Both Nehru and Bhabha regarded science and technology as powerful instruments of economic and social transformation. The scale of the government’s investment in scientific research reflected this commitment. In Science and Technology in India (1977), Keswani writes: “It was Nehru’s government which lifted Indian science from its small beginnings to a national effort. The Indian government spent Rs. 550 million on research in 1964, the year of Nehru’s death. In 1947, it was merely Rs. 24 million.”

Why ‘scientific temper’ mattered to Nehru

Story continues below this ad

For Nehru, science was not merely a body of knowledge or a means of technological advancement, but a way of approaching life’s problems. 

In Volume 9 of Selected works of Jawaharlal Nehru, he explained: “What is science? It is a certain way of approaching problems, a certain way of seeking the truth. It is a certain empirical way whereby we get prepared to reject anything if we cannot establish or prove it.” 

Also Read | Why Nehru supported China’s bid for UNSC seat, over offers to India from the US and the USSR

“What I wish to emphasise is that science means an approach to all of life’s problems. It is to be applied to the problems relating to our family, religion and everything else. You cannot apply science in your industries keeping other departments of your life free from it. The whole scheme is unscientific. Therefore, if we want to consider various problems that face us as an individual and as a social group, the right way to consider these problems is to adopt the method of science.”

Nehru also saw socialism through this lens, explaining his own political convictions in terms of a scientific approach to social problems: “I am a socialist because I feel that socialism is a scientific approach to the world’s problems. It is not necessary that I should agree with every other socialist but generally a socialist approach is scientific and that appeals to me tremendously.”

Where science and religion meet

Story continues below this ad

Nehru believed that religious thought, too, had to be compatible with reason and scientific inquiry. In his words, “Dharma is good so long as it does not get into conflict with the rational or scientific attitude.” Nehru’s appreciation of Buddhism, according to Keswani, was partly rooted in his understanding of it as a rational tradition. “He averred that Buddha’s method was one of psychological analysis and that Buddha had insight in the latest methods of science.”

Also Read | When Nehru moved resolution that became basis for Preamble: ‘This House cannot bind down the next generation’

In a speech cited in Volume 14 (1) of Selected works of Jawaharlal Nehru, Nehru cautioned against reducing both religion and science to outward forms and practices: “Religion became a set of ceremonials and forms and some kind of a ritual worship. The inner spirit left the people. Large numbers of people talk glibly about science today and yet in their lives or actions do not exhibit a trace of science. They think of science as some isolated area where there are test tubes and other mechanical appliances but have no other relation to life, except sometimes to provide them some conveniences… But science is something more. It is a way of training the mind to look at life and the whole social structure. If science is truth then you must follow that truth. So I stress the need for the development of a scientific mind and temper which is more important than actual discovery as it is out of this temper and method that many more discoveries will come…”

title: How hackers took control of supermarket fridges across Europe, and what it means for India’s cold chain
content_html:
Refrigerated display cases at a Meny supermarket in Bergen, Norway, in 2017. Recent cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems elsewhere in Europe have highlighted the risks of connecting cooling equipment to the internet. (Wikimedia Commons)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Overnight on October 11–12, hackers took control of refrigeration systems at around 700 retail sites in France, including stores run by Carrefour and Intermarché. They turned up the temperature settings used to melt ice off the cooling coils, causing food to spoil and starting at least 15 fires, according to France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI.

A second wave of such attacks followed in early November, affecting stores in eight European countries, including Belgium, Sweden and Ireland, and forcing retailers to throw away large quantities of food. Separately, an attack on a refrigeration equipment supplier affected the systems that monitor and control temperatures at three sites of France’s national blood service. Its alarm systems alerted staff, who moved the blood products before any were lost.

On November 9, France accused Shahid Kaveh, a unit linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), of orchestrating the October attacks, a charge Iran has denied. Authorities have not established that the subsequent incidents were carried out by the same group.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Refrigeration keeps food and medical supplies at safe temperatures as they are stored, transported and distributed. That temperature-controlled system is known as the cold chain. Connecting cooling equipment to the internet lets operators check temperatures, spot faults and adjust settings remotely. The attacks showed what can happen when someone else gains access to those controls.

First, how do cold storage systems work?

A cold-storage facility is a large, insulated refrigerator, often divided into rooms maintained at different temperatures depending on what is stored inside. Its insulated walls slow the entry of heat from outside, while refrigeration equipment continuously removes the heat that gets in. This preserves everything from fresh fruits and vegetables to frozen food, vaccines and blood products.

But how does a refrigerator actually cool a room?

It uses a refrigerant, a substance that circulates through pipes and changes between liquid and gas. As it passes through cooling coils inside the storage area, it absorbs heat from the surrounding air. A compressor raises the pressure and temperature of the refrigerant, which then releases heat through a second set of coils outside the cooled space.

Maintaining the required temperature involves constant monitoring. Sensors measure the temperature and send readings to an electronic controller. In industrial facilities, this may be a programmable logic controller (PLC), a rugged industrial computer that sends instructions to equipment such as compressors, fans and pumps.

Story continues below this ad

For instance, when a loading door opens and warmer air enters, the sensors detect the resulting temperature change. The controller can then adjust the cooling equipment to bring the room back to the required temperature. It also manages defrost cycles, during which ice accumulated on the cooling coils is periodically melted. Without this process, ice can obstruct airflow and reduce cooling efficiency.

So, why connect refrigerators to the internet?

Traditionally, staff checked and recorded temperatures by hand. Connecting refrigerators to the internet allows businesses to monitor their performance remotely and manage several facilities through a single system.

“Businesses connect refrigerators to the internet to monitor temperatures and equipment performance in real time, receive alerts before stock spoils, diagnose faults remotely and manage many sites from one system,” Sandeep Kachhawa, an energy efficiency researcher, told The Indian Express.

Such equipment is part of the Internet of Things (IoT), where physical devices, including sensors and controllers, exchange information over a network.

Story continues below this ad
Also in Explained | Microsoft global outage: How one cloud failure disrupted businesses worldwide

Connected systems “also allow authorised staff or service providers to adjust temperature settings, alarm thresholds or defrost cycles remotely,” Kachhawa said “This improves response times, but creates a cyber risk if the controller is poorly secured.”

How can a cyberattack disrupt refrigeration?

Refrigeration controllers can become vulnerable when they are directly exposed to the internet or accessed through poorly secured remote connections. Attackers can identify such equipment online and attempt to gain access using weak or default passwords, or exploit vulnerabilities in outdated software.

“Many legacy systems used in Pharma, hospitals and industrial cold chains may have internet connectivity to enable monitoring and remote access so suppliers can undertake remote diagnostics,” Arun Rajagopal, principal consultant and managing partner at Cyber Forte UK, told The Indian Express.

Such connections could also allow attackers to move from an organisation’s corporate network into the systems controlling its physical equipment. “Time and time again, past security incidents have shown how easy it is for an attacker to pivot from Corporate IT Networks to OT or Industrial Environments,” Rajagopal said.

Story continues below this ad

The risks are compounded by the long lifespan of industrial equipment. Xavier Bellekens, CEO of cybersecurity firm Lupovis, pointed out that while laptops might be replaced every three to five years, refrigeration equipment can remain operational for 15–20 years, sometimes long after manufacturers stop providing software security updates.

“The equipment may still work perfectly from a mechanical perspective, even though its software is outdated and its manufacturer no longer provides security updates,” he said.

Lupovis observed suspicious activity against its simulated Danfoss refrigeration controllers, known as honeypots, between October 20 and 30, following the first wave of attacks in France. These systems replicate real equipment, allowing researchers to observe attackers without exposing actual facilities.

“Over this ten-day period, we identified more than 250 attempts from 91 distinct sources, with activity peaking on 26 October,” Bellekens told The Indian Express. The attackers attempted to log in using default credentials and probed the controllers for vulnerabilities.

Story continues below this ad

Bellekens had earlier told POLITICO that the activity could be linked to a Russian state-sponsored group, citing infrastructure previously associated with Russian hackers. Russia has denied involvement.

“We believe this activity may represent preparation for the second wave, but definitive attribution would require further investigation,” Bellekens told The Indian Express.

What could an attack mean for food supplies?

Farmers could lose income if their produce spoils or buyers cannot collect it. Food processors, retailers and logistics companies could face stock losses and supply delays, while consumers could experience shortages or higher prices.

Also Read | What is PHP2Shell, and why did it force websites around the world offline?

“An attack on an individual facility would be unlikely to cause a nationwide food crisis, but disruption to a major distribution hub could affect supplies across several cities or regions,” Kachhawa said.

Story continues below this ad

“If several facilities use the same refrigeration controls and automation vendor, a security weakness could affect multiple sites. This could turn a problem at one supplier or platform into a wider disruption,” he added. However, he cautioned that using the same technology does not automatically make every facility vulnerable; the security of the systems and their remote connections matters.

What does this mean for India’s cold chain?

India had 8,831 cold-storage facilities with a combined capacity of about 40.3 million metric tonnes, the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare said in a response to a Rajya Sabha question on February 6, 2026.

As these facilities adopt more automated and remotely monitored systems, they could also become exposed to the vulnerabilities seen in Europe.

In India, the risk is likely to be concentrated in cold-chain facilities that use internet-connected refrigeration controls, remote monitoring and external vendor access, Kachhawa said. These include organised retail chains, dairy chilling facilities, pharmaceutical warehouses, vaccine storage centres and large distribution hubs. Refrigerated transport may also be vulnerable where trucks use connected temperature-monitoring and fleet-management systems.

Story continues below this ad

The exposure, however, is not uniform. Traditional potato cold storage facilities are less exposed to remote cyberattacks because most of their equipment is locally controlled and not connected to external networks, Kachhawa said.

Who is responsible for keeping these systems safe?

According to Arun Rajagopal, securing connected refrigeration systems is a shared responsibility, involving equipment manufacturers, software providers, maintenance contractors and the businesses operating them.

“This is a shared responsibility between product manufacturers, system integrators and asset owners and operators,” Rajagopal said. He pointed to network and information security rules in the UK and EU for operators, and to the EU Cyber Resilience Act’s requirements for product suppliers.

Manufacturers are responsible for secure equipment and software updates, while operators must monitor which devices are connected and who can access them.

Story continues below this ad

For older equipment that no longer receives security updates, Bellekens said operators need additional protections rather than necessarily replacing entire refrigeration installations. “However, it must recognise that the controller presents a risk and restrict access to it accordingly.”

India is also encouraging greater automation in cold-chain infrastructure. The National Centre for Cold-chain Development’s (NCCD) Engineering Guidelines & Minimum System Standards (2025) encourage IoT-based monitoring, remote control and unified control systems for facilities supported under central government schemes.

However, Kachhawa said the guidelines do not appear to specify detailed cybersecurity requirements for these connected systems, including secure remote access, network separation, user authentication and software updates.

Separately, CERT-In’s May 2026 cybersecurity blueprint identifies operational technology (OT), which controls physical equipment, and cyber-physical systems as areas requiring protection. Its recommendations include restricting remote access, monitoring third-party vendors and managing supply-chain risks.

What should operators do? Rajagopal stressed the importance of strong passwords, multi-factor authentication and keeping critical controllers off the public internet.

“Cybersecurity and safety trumps operational flexibility,” he said.

Kachhawa also recommended independent temperature sensors and alarms, alongside procedures for manually monitoring temperatures and moving products if automated controls fail.

The French blood-service incident demonstrated why such precautions matter: its alarms detected abnormal temperature changes, allowing staff to move blood products before they were lost.

At the policy level, Kachhawa called for cybersecurity requirements to be incorporated into cold-chain infrastructure standards and government funding conditions, alongside regular assessments of facilities storing essential food and medical products.

The Indian Express
.

“An attack on an individual facility would be unlikely to cause a nationwide food crisis, but disruption to a major distribution hub could affect supplies across several cities or regions,” Kachhawa said.

Rajya Sabha
question on February 6, 2026.

Who is responsible for keeping these systems safe?
According to Arun Rajagopal, securing connected refrigeration systems is a shared responsibility, involving equipment manufacturers, software providers, maintenance contractors and the businesses operating them.
“This is a shared responsibility between product manufacturers, system integrators and asset owners and operators,” Rajagopal said. He pointed to network and information security rules in the UK and EU for operators, and to the EU Cyber Resilience Act’s requirements for product suppliers.
Manufacturers are responsible for secure equipment and software updates, while operators must monitor which devices are connected and who can access them.

For older equipment that no longer receives security updates, Bellekens said operators need additional protections rather than necessarily replacing entire refrigeration installations. “However, it must recognise that the controller presents a risk and restrict access to it accordingly.”

India is also encouraging greater automation in cold-chain infrastructure. However, Kachhawa said the guidelines do not appear to specify detailed cybersecurity requirements for these connected systems, including secure remote access, network separation, user authentication and software updates.

Its recommendations include restricting remote access, monitoring third-party vendors and managing supply-chain risks.
What should operators do? Rajagopal stressed the importance of strong passwords, multi-factor authentication and keeping critical controllers off the public internet.
“Cybersecurity and safety trumps operational flexibility,” he said.
Kachhawa also recommended independent temperature sensors and alarms, alongside procedures for manually monitoring temperatures and moving products if automated controls fail.
The French blood-service incident demonstrated why such precautions matter: its alarms detected abnormal temperature changes, allowing staff to move blood products before they were lost.
At the policy level, Kachhawa called for cybersecurity requirements to be incorporated into cold-chain infrastructure standards and government funding conditions, alongside regular assessments of facilities storing essential food and medical products.

title: Expert Explains | COP31: What’s at stake at UN climate summit in Antalya
content_html:
A sign for the COP31 UN Climate Summit at the Istanbul Airport in Turkey. Photo: AP/Emrah Gurel/File

Written by Indu K Murthy

Starting Monday (November 9), the next chapter of global climate action will unfold in Turkey at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) until November 20, with about 100,000 participants and heads of state gathering for a World Leaders’ Summit on November 11 and 12.

As the first COP since the United States’ exit from the Paris Agreement earlier this year, COP31 removes the largest historical emitter from finance conversations, sharpening developing countries’ demand that Europe and others fill the gap. Energy security, meanwhile, has taken centre stage. The war on Iran has pushed up oil and gas prices, raising the cost of fuel and food. Supporters of a faster energy transition argue that this shows the risks of fossil-fuel dependence, while importers such as India face more immediate pressure to keep supplies affordable.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The questions that matter are how much finance will actually flow to developing countries, how adaptation will be measured and paid for, and whether mounting pressure on coal and emission targets will respect the principle of “common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities” (CBDR-RC).

What is a COP?

A COP is the annual meeting of countries that signed the 1992 UNFCCC. In Antalya, there will be three meetings in focus: COP31, the 21st session of the Conference of Parties serving as the meeting of Parties to the Kyoto Protocol (CMP21), and the 8th session of the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of Parties to the 2015 Paris Agreement (CMA8).

Also read | Three steps COP should take for tangible outcomes

The Paris Agreement asks every country to submit a nationally determined contribution (NDC), essentially its own climate plan, every five years, with the shared ambition of holding warming well below 2°C while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Because decisions require consensus, a single country can hold up an agreement.

How is COP31 different from previous COPs?

COP venues rotate among the UN’s regional groups, and 2026 was the turn of the “Western European and Others” group to host. Turkey bid with Antalya, and Australia bid with Adelaide, in partnership with Pacific Island nations.

Story continues below this ad

The resulting standoff led to an unusual power-sharing deal last year, making COP31 the first summit where one country hosts the meeting while another runs the negotiations.

Turkey is the formal COP31 president and host, responsible for the venue, logistics, and the “Action Agenda” of voluntary pledges and initiatives, whereas Australia has “exclusive authority” over formal talks, drafting of texts, and steering decisions. This dual leadership model is untested, and questions remain about who would have the final word if there were disagreement in the closing hours. 

What’s on the table?

COP31 is not expected to produce a landmark treaty text. The real fight is over delivery: mobilising finance, measuring progress, and accelerating the energy shift.

In terms of co-chairing consultations, India and Germany must decide on mitigation, as in how to press countries whose 2035 plans fall short of 1.5°C and what “transitioning away from fossil fuels” actually requires. On finance, France and the Philippines will work to build consensus on delivering existing finance commitments. On adaptation, the UK and Sierra Leone must chart a credible path to tripling adaptation finance and make enough headway for the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) to be finalised at COP32.

Story continues below this ad
A street vendor walks amid thick haze from wildfires in Indonesia on October 24, 2026. Photo: AP/Yulianus Stefan Lundju/File

Taking on newer ground, Mexico and Poland must work out how the just transition mechanism will function and what money and technical help it will give affected workers and communities. Palau and Canada handle the ocean, where Pacific Island countries want commitments written into formal decisions.

Two more items will set the summit’s tone. Turkey wants countries to pledge to raise electricity’s share of global final energy use from about 23% today to 35% by 2035. Further, developing countries, including India, have pushed to include Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, the clause that obligates developed countries to provide finance, in the provisional agenda.

What Belém left behind

The COP30 in Belém, Brazil, closed with a package called the “Global Mutirão” (meaning, collective effort) and Antalya inherits this “to-do” list. It called for adaptation finance to be at least tripled by 2035, five years later than developing countries had wanted and without a clear baseline.

More broadly, it endorsed the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap to scale climate finance for developing countries to at least $1.3 trillion a year by 2035 from public and private sources, building on the $300 billion-a-year goal agreed at COP29 in Baku (Azerbaijan). It adopted a set of “Belém indicators” to measure progress on the GGA, created new vehicles for delivery, namely a Global Implementation Accelerator and a “Belém Mission to 1.5” to help countries carry out their plans, alongside work on a just transition mechanism.

Story continues below this ad
Also read | Look beyond old climate fault lines

The most conspicuous gap concerned fossil fuels. More than 80 countries backed a roadmap to move away from oil, coal, and gas, yet the final text left fossil fuels out entirely, referring only to the 2023 Dubai “UAE Consensus”. Brazil is now steering a voluntary roadmap process outside the formal talks, and Colombia and the Netherlands have initiated the Santa Marta process — an international, plurilateral climate initiative complementing the COP process launched in Santa Marta, Colombia — in April 2026 to identify pathways for the phase-out.

Where does India stand on its climate goals?

India goes to Antalya with a new climate plan and a central seat at the table, co-chairing mitigation consultations. India’s third NDC, covering 2031-2035, was approved and submitted in April.

The new plan raises the target for reducing the emission intensity of gross domestic product (GDP) to 47% below 2005 levels by 2035, up from 45% by 2030. Emission intensity of GDP, which measures the volume of greenhouse gases (usually carbon dioxide, or CO2, equivalent) emitted for each unit of economic output or GDP, acts as a key indicator of how carbon-efficient an economy is as it grows.

The plan increases the non-fossil share of installed power capacity from 50% by 2030 (already met) to 60% by 2035 and expands the promised additional carbon sink from forest and tree cover from 2.5-3.0 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent to 3.5-4.0 billion tonnes. A carbon sink refers to any natural or artificial system that absorbs more CO2 from the atmosphere than it releases, helping reduce the greenhouse gases responsible for global warming.

Story continues below this ad
Also read | India must set a higher bar on clean energy targets

The NDC, however, ties any further ambition to “new and additional” finance and technology from developed countries. This conditionality runs through India’s negotiating line, which Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Bhupender Yadav set out at the Pre-COP in Fiji last month (October 5-8, 2026).

Yadav called for equal weight to be given to adaptation; mitigation; and the “means of implementation”, that is, finance, technology, and capacity-building. He insisted that the principle of CBDR-RC be upheld “in letter and spirit”, with no one-size-fits-all pathway imposed on countries. He backed the Article 9.1 finance discussion and argued that success should be measured by delivery on existing commitments rather than by new targets or declarations.

COP31: What to watch out for

Five questions will determine how Antalya is remembered.

The first is finance, and whether developed countries put numbers and a timeline behind tripling adaptation finance and give the $1.3 trillion roadmap a monitoring system.
The second is fossil fuels, and whether the negotiated text will include a transition away from them.

Story continues below this ad

The third is Turkey’s electrification pledge, specifically how many countries sign on to the 35%-by-2035 target.

The fourth is the split presidency itself — the real stress test of a model that future COPs may copy.

The fifth is the Global South bargain, and whether India and other developing countries secure the Article 9.1 discussion and reforms to finance access in return for engaging on mitigation.

Ultimately, Antalya will be judged less on headline pledges and more on whether the promises of Paris, Baku, and Belém translate into meaningful action.

Story continues below this ad

The author heads the climate, environment and sustainability sector at the Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP), a research-based think tank.

title: Decoding the 2026 US midterms verdict: Why Delhi must rediscover and engage with the many Americas
content_html:
The Democratic Party’s sweeping victory in the American midterm elections presents India with immediate and long-term imperatives in dealing with the United States, its most important and comprehensive partner for the foreseeable future.

The immediate task is to step up engagement with the Trump administration, wrap up the long-pending bilateral trade agreement and advance cooperation in energy, defence and technology.

Advertisement

The latest election is part of the enduring ebb and flow of American politics. The Democratic triumph this week does not guarantee it victory in the 2028 presidential election or continued Congressional domination in the next congressional cycle. Instead of obsessing with mood swings in the American electorate, Delhi must rediscover America’s extraordinary political diversity and rebuild relationships across its rapidly changing political landscape.

It is not just Trump who will fade from the scene in the coming years. Familiar Democratic figures — the Clintons, Obama and Biden — are also yielding to a new generation representing a more diverse America. If India was surprised by the power of the MAGA movement on the right, it must prepare for potential shocks from the rise of progressive forces on the Democratic side.

More immediately, Prime Minister Narendra Modi could have two opportunities to meet Trump — at the East Asia Summit in Manila this month and the G20 summit in Miami in December. These encounters offer Delhi an opportunity to consolidate the partnership after a turbulent period. Trump will remain in office for more than two years and retain considerable authority over foreign policy until his last day in the White House.

Challenges for India’s political class

Advertisement

For the Indian political class, the long-term challenge is threefold.

First, move away from a shallow understanding of America (Republicans are “good”, Democrats are “bad” or vice versa) and an emotional reaction to developments (every remark by an official in DC gets amplified into some kind of a turning point in relations). We need a better appreciation of America’s deep structures, its changing internal dynamics, and their impact on US policies.

Neither the Republican nor the Democratic Party has a settled ideological identity, and divisions within them are often as sharp as those between them. Shifting coalitions across party lines increasingly shape American policies at home and abroad. Grasping the multiple strands of American politics and its changing coalitions is key to successful policy formulation in Delhi.

Also in Explained | US midterms: Key takeaways, impact on the world and India

Second, discard the assumption that Washington needs Delhi more than India needs America. This encouraged needless complacency, which Trump’s second term shattered. A more realistic appreciation of what binds and divides the two countries is essential for stable engagement.

Third, return to the diplomatic playbook that transformed bilateral relations in the 1990s and 2000s. That transformation did not emerge simply from agreements between presidents and prime ministers. It involved patient efforts to seek and win friends across Congress, business, universities, think tanks and the Indian diaspora.

The historic civil nuclear agreement of 2008 was the culmination of a diplomatic playbook that transformed bilateral India-US relations in the 1990s and 2000s. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

The historic civil nuclear agreement of 2008 was the culmination of that effort. It required full backing from the White House, bipartisan support in Congress. It demanded the readiness to engage sceptics and overcome entrenched opposition. Delhi did not assume India’s strategic importance would automatically produce favourable outcomes in Washington. It invested political and diplomatic capital in building a supportive coalition.

That lesson is especially relevant today. America’s federal structure, a powerful legislature, corporations, universities, media and civic organisations create multiple centres of political influence. American politics is not merely a contest between Republicans and Democrats, but a continuing negotiation among competing economic interests, regional identities and ideological traditions.

Transformations within Republicans, Democrats

Trump’s nationalist movement has transformed the Republican Party, challenging traditional commitments to free trade, immigration and international alliances. Yet the party remains divided between economic nationalists, market-oriented libertarians, religious conservatives, and those seeking an end to endless wars.

The Democrats are undergoing an equally consequential transformation. Progressives challenge traditional leaders on inequality, corporate power, defence spending, and foreign policy. Divisions over Israel, the Middle East and military intervention reflect a wider struggle over the party’s international outlook. Anti-war movements on the left share some ground with isolationist sentiments on the right. The midterm results will intensify these debates as both parties prepare for the 2028 presidential contest.

Delhi cannot afford to remain confined to established networks. The task is not merely to cultivate those sympathetic to India, but also to engage critics on trade, immigration, human rights and Russia. India has lost friends among American progressives, and a special effort is needed to reconnect with them. Changing demographics, the growing influence of ethnic minorities and the revival of socialist traditions demand greater Indian attention to the American left.

More in Explained | US midterms: What the setback for Trump means for US-India trade deal

This task cannot be left to the government alone. Indian political parties, civil society and business must deepen engagement with their American counterparts. The BJP and RSS are developing their own independent outreach to America. Rahul Gandhi has frequently travelled to the US, but Congress needs more structured engagement with American society. Indian parties must reach beyond the diaspora to the wider forces shaping American polity.

India will continue to need the American partnership for economic transformation, technological modernisation and regional security. But it cannot rely merely on personal chemistry between leaders or relations between governments of the moment. India needs not just strong ties with the White House, the permanent bureaucracy and Congress, but also a broad and durable constituency of friends across the many Americas.

The author is a contributing editor on international affairs for The Indian Express.

Edited excerpts from the Explained.Live interview.

What was holding the markets back?

One is Indian promoters who have been launching IPO after IPO because they know that the markets are overvalued. The second is private equity companies which had invested pre-2023, which had realised that you can sell these stocks to Indian investors at a good price. And the third was multinationals who had set up businesses in India over the last 20, 30, 40 years. They realised that they should list in India because here you get valuations much higher than in your home country.

Despite the huge amount of money that we collected, all that money primarily went into these three sets of people’s pockets. And that is why markets have not delivered returns.

But AI can be a structural trend. And no one knows what the long-term impact of AI will be. People believe that fund managers can correctly guess the long-term impact, but we also don’t know. 

Story continues below this ad

There is a talk of India becoming a $20-trillion economy say two decades from now. Are the grounds ready for that?

In the services sector, there are no other countries which are competing with us. In manufacturing, there are multiple countries that are competing, including Vietnam and Thailand.

To win in manufacturing is not as easy as winning in services. Is India working to become better every year over the previous year? Yes. But the competition is intense.

I think we need to create manufacturing employment on a very very large scale. And that is the solution for growth to increase. And I’m sure that the government is well aware of this issue and will focus on it. But it is not as easy to create a global manufacturing hub in every area as it has been to create a global services hub.

You just keep investing in these categories and keep saving and keeping put money in these three categories because our broad approach is very clear.

Balanced advantage is a very simple model: As the market goes up, you keep selling, and as the market goes down, you keep buying. So in 2023-24 when the market was more overvalued, it had less exposure to equity and higher exposure to debt and arbitrage. Today, because equity has become more fairly valued, it has a higher exposure to equity and a lower exposure to arbitrage and debt.

If you look at balanced hybrids, it’s even more simple. It says you can invest between 40% and 60% in debt, and 40% and 60% in equity. It is the quintessential asset allocation product where you’re choosing two products, and both the products have to be between 40% and 60%. 

The third category is called “flexi” cap because you can invest in all kinds of things. You can invest in large cap, mid cap, small cap, micro cap and, therefore, you are entirely investing in the entire equity market. So we call it the most unconstrained fund.

For people who need gold, I would say multi-asset is the fourth category.

For the first 10 years of people’s investing career, they should choose mutual funds so that they go through one cycle. They understand what is investing through balanced advantage or multi asset or flexi cap. After 10 years of investing, if you have learned quite a lot, then you do direct equity. And if you become an expert after 20, 30 years, you do derivatives.

But unfortunately, when we talk to stockbrokers, they say it is 25 to 30-year-olds who are actually trading derivatives. I do not know whether they have the knowledge and the temperament to handle it well.

Reader questions

Countries which have AI on their side, like the US, their markets are doing much better. Would you suggest that we try to invest in foreign markets?

Any market which is exuberant and where valuations are high is actually a riskier market. So, at this point of time we tell people to be careful if you are investing in the Nasdaq index because it is the best performing index in the world in the last 10 years. 

I am currently investing in mutual funds. My SIP is around Rs 25,000 a month. Should I stop it because for the past 2 years, whatever I have invested giving negative returns?

We tell people to start a SIP in flexi cap category or balanced advantage category or multi-asset category. Forget closing, we tell people to add now. That is our view. Actually, that is what we have been trying to promote at this point of time. So, I think you know, for the best benefit of SIP, you actually have to invest when the markets are down.

title: After US midterm wipeout, will Trump resume Iran war? An expert explains
content_html:
The US midterm polls have left the Democratic Party in firm control of both Houses of the US Congress, with the Republican Party suffering historic losses even in traditional strongholds.

Behind the Blue Tsunami was the cost of living crisis in the US, exacerbated by President Donald Trump’s tariffs and, crucially, the war he started against Iran — which drove up fuel prices domestically and globally.

Advertisement

Indeed, after the results, Vice President J D Vance acknowledged on X that “the reason we lost is the war [with Iran]”. Trump has himself called this “largely true”.

The question now is whether a defeated Trump will lash out by resuming the war with Iran or pursue a deal instead.

The signals seem mixed. Early after the polls, he seemed disinclined towards more war, saying: “We seem to be getting everything we want… we’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it.”

Advertisement

But, on Thursday, he tried to keep the possibility open: “Do we want to go further (with military action)? I would rather not destroy the rest of the country, if possible, but maybe I will have to. You’ll know soon enough.”

US President Donald Trump faces a dilemma over how to deal with Iran. (AP)

Vance, perhaps driven by the need to distance himself from Trump before the 2028 Presidential elections, has been clearer. He said that for voters to return to the party, the administration would have to “end the war, focus on inflation, put America first (and) change our relationship to Israel”.

With the new Congress set to take office in early January, the US now appears simultaneously on the verge of both war and a deal with Iran. What are the pathways ahead?

The path to war

As has been explained before in these columns, the Trump administration’s military actions against Iran later in the year were essentially an attempt to improve its bargaining position for a deal. But this prolonged entanglement in West Asia has significantly affected its domestic standing, as proved by the midterm polls. The President’s approval rating now stands at 38%.

In recent months, Vance has reportedly privately accused Israel’s (now caretaker) Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, of being “wrong on everything” about Iran. This shows Washington DC’s loss of faith in the military approach that has long been pushed by the Israeli leader.

Also Read | US midterms: Trump loses Congress. What changes for India and the world?

If anything, the US’s post-midterms predicament has strengthened Tehran’s bargaining position, reflected in Iranian leaders’ rhetoric following the results. This, in turn, may force the US President to save face through yet another visible show of force, even if a deal remains the ultimate objective.

But Trump’s principal challenge, even before the midterms, has been that Tehran retains as much agency as Washington in determining when a round of strikes ends.

US Vice President JD Vance has been trying to distance himself from Trump. (AP)

In the run-up to the polls and ever since, Tehran has consistently asserted that there is not a single US military pathway — whether swift or prolonged — that will not result in escalatory retaliation, especially with potentially longer-range missiles being used without “geographic restraint”.

This significantly cuts into Washington’s space for calibrated military action that absorbs the cost of Iranian retaliation but still keeps Tehran at the table.

The regional Arab states, which faced the brunt of Iran’s retaliatory attacks earlier this year, know that another round of fighting will hobble them economically. Recognising both Washington’s dilemma and Tehran’s resilience, Qatar, Turkey, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and UAE are proactively pushing for any possible interim arrangement.

Also Read | Democrats flip both Houses in midterms: What happens next in Trump’s Washington?

The US achieved no strategic objective through the war it started with Israel in late February. Resuming it would do even less for its bargaining position in the ongoing negotiations for an interim deal.

The path to a deal

In the run-up to the midterms, it was the aforementioned lack of an achievable objective that prevented US military action, or support for Israeli action.

Iran remains interested in forcing the US to return to the core terms of the collapsed interim peace deal from June. This is reflected in its seven demands — including cessation of hostilities, end of the US blockade, sanctions relief, release of frozen Iranian funds and reparations, among others.

Also Read | Decoding the 2026 US midterms verdict: Why Delhi must rediscover and engage with the many Americas

Iran also wishes to retain the pathway to peace that was set out in the June memorandum of understanding — the US meeting these seven demands, followed by Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz (retaining the right to coordinate shipping with Oman), and then both sides then moving to nuclear talks.

For Tehran, this interest supersedes the need to preempt hostilities with Washington (as it has rhetorically been threatening to do).

A banner depicting Iran’s late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in central Tehran on Tuesday, (November 3). (AP)

Iran refrained from responding to Israel’s large-scale aerial provocation close to Iranian airspace in October. It is also now reportedly amenable to a two-day implementation window for an interim deal — Day 1 would see Iran admitting International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors in return for a lifting of the US blockade and release of frozen Iranian funds; Day 2 would see Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and the initiation of talks over its reported 440 kg stockpile of 60% enriched uranium.

This is a marked step-down from Iran’s seven-day roadmap presented to the US in September.

Also Read | Trump says US will cut military aid to Israel: Why now, and what can actually happen?

However, if the midterm results dissuade the Trump administration from military action, it would need Iranian nuclear concessions (related to the 60% enriched uranium) even in the interim deal.

This is unlike the June MoU, which effectively agreed to defer nuclear negotiations for 60 days. This is untenable for Tehran, especially as it blames Washington for undermining key provisions of the June MoU, such as guaranteeing Iranian/Omani control of the Strait of Hormuz.

The clock is ticking

For the Trump administration, time is running out for a smooth path to removing sanctions on Iran — a core part of Tehran’s demands.

On September 18, Trump had signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. This statute had extended the expiry of the original 1996 Iran Sanctions Act from December 2026 to December 2031. For permanent sanctions relief, a Congressional vote is inevitable.

Also Read | Who will form Israel government? The three scenarios involving Eisenkot and Netanyahu

Moreover, it was a Republican-led House and Senate which had passed the 2015 Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act that sought to review Barack Obama’s nuclear deal. Now, this same Act binds the Trump administration to submit any nuclear deal with Iran to Congress with a 60-day review period. For a Republican-led Congress to oversee this review period, a comprehensive deal for full sanctions relief would ideally need to have been submitted by November 7.

Hence, notwithstanding the actual complexity of Congress-linked options facing President Trump for whenever a nuclear deal is on the table, an interim agreement remains the only viable path presently.

But Trump is not the only one facing the difficult question of releasing funds to Iran. Democrats, too, will soon have to choose — back a Trump-led deal, or be seen as prolonging the war. That, however, remains a problem for after January, when the new Democrat-controlled Congress takes charge.

Also Read | A third front in US politics: Reading the rise of Democratic Socialists in capitalist USA

Ironically, it is also this closing “lame duck” window which arguably presents the last opportunity for Washington to attempt another military-led attempt at forcing early nuclear concessions from Tehran.

Ultimately, it will be Iran’s willingness (or lack thereof) to offer nuclear concessions during an interim deal that will determine whether Washington turns to the military to save face.

This is notwithstanding a ‘Black Swan’ scenario where Israeli caretaker PM Netanyahu or his successor conducts fresh unilateral strikes on Iran and allows Washington to intervene, declare a ceasefire, and secure credit for “ending” the war — which it had started.

Ironically, it is also this closing “lame duck” window which arguably presents the last opportunity for Washington to attempt another military-led attempt at forcing early nuclear concessions from Tehran.
Ultimately, it will be Iran’s willingness (or lack thereof) to offer nuclear concessions during an interim deal that will determine whether Washington turns to the military to save face.
This is notwithstanding a ‘Black Swan’ scenario where Israeli caretaker PM Netanyahu or his successor conducts fresh unilateral strikes on Iran and allows Washington to intervene, declare a ceasefire, and secure credit for “ending” the war — which it had started.

title: Why India should observe China’s Fifth Plenum, as Xi Jinping tightens political control
content_html:
Chinese President Xi Jinping, center attends a meeting at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, China. (Kai Naito/Pool Photo via AP)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

A key political meeting that recently concluded in China reflected President Xi Jinping’s resolve to tighten political control and reinforce the supremacy of the Communist Party of China (CPC).

The Fifth Plenary Session of the Party’s 20th Central Committee, held in Beijing from October 26–29, also addressed institutional vulnerabilities, which matter ahead of next year’s Party Congress — an all-important meeting held every five years. According to the official communiqué, the conclave focused on internal Party discipline, leadership adjustments, and preparations for the next political cycle.

For India, the implications are strategic rather than merely political. Understanding China requires looking beyond its economic strength and military hardware to its political architecture, the mindset of its leadership, and strategic behaviour.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Significance of the Plenums

During its five-year tenure, the CPC Central Committee, elected by the National Party Congress (NPC) or the national legislature, holds seven plenary sessions. These serve as important instruments for translating the NPC’s political directions into policies and decisions.

Although each plenum follows an established agenda, the 20th Central Committee (established during the 2022 Party Congress) witnessed some deviations. The First and Second Plenums focus on top leadership appointments and state institutional structures. The Third Plenum addresses major economic policies and reforms; this time delayed and held in July 2024.

Also in Explained | How Xi Jinping’s sweeping military purge echoed at a top Chinese leaders’ meeting

The Fourth Plenum, associated with Party building, was held in October 2025 and took up the task of finalising guidelines for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030), an exercise normally reserved for the Fifth Plenum. Consequently, the Fifth Plenum shifted its emphasis towards strengthening CPC governance structures ahead of the 2027 Party Congress. The Sixth traditionally centres on ideology and Party discipline, while the Seventh prepares the agenda for the next NPC.

The Fifth Plenum must be viewed against the evolution of Xi’s leadership since 2012. Anti-corruption and Party discipline have been defining features of his tenure. The 20th Party Congress in October 2022 consolidated Xi Jinping’s position as China’s paramount political leader and reaffirmed his vision of national modernisation and rejuvenation. His term as the general secretary, or top leader, of the CPC was extended for a historic third time.

Story continues below this ad

The record-low attendance at the latest meeting also came amid continuing leadership upheaval, marked by investigations and disciplinary action against civilian officials and People’s Liberation Army (PLA) commanders.

Fifth Plenum: Highlights and key outcomes

The communiqué outlined several guiding principles, including strengthening of Party leadership, enforcing rigorous governance across organisations, improving institutional oversight and ensuring governance through Party regulations.

Opinion | In the name of discipline, Xi has centralised power further

A consequential outcome was the adoption of a resolution reinforcing the CPC’s position that its capacity to govern itself is fundamental to its ability to govern China. The emphasis on top-down control was particularly significant.

Perhaps the most consequential development remains the continuing upheaval within the PLA. The Plenum confirmed the expulsion of 33 officials from the Party. These included senior military figures such as Zhang Youxia, former Vice Chairman of the apex military decision-making body, the Central Military Commission (CMC), Liu Zhenli, former Chief of Staff of the Joint Staff Department, Ma Xingrui, former Politburo member and Wang Haijiang, former Western Theatre Commander. This theatre also concerns the border with India.

Story continues below this ad

The shrinking military leadership is evident from the CMC’s composition. Constituted with seven members in 2022, it has since seen five members removed, leaving only Xi as Chairman and General Zhang Shengmin, who oversees military discipline. The Plenum did not announce appointments to fill the vacant positions. This could reflect an effort to retain direct control and avoid potential internal challenges, particularly amid suspicions concerning officers associated with the purged figures.

The political signal

The Plenum formally announced that the 21st Party Congress would be held in Beijing in the latter half of October 2027. It will determine the composition of the CPC’s senior leadership for the next five-year cycle.

Xi’s position remains firmly at the centre of the political system and he is widely expected to seek another term. No succession arrangements have been announced. In China’s opaque political system, personnel changes and purges offer important, though not definitive, indicators of leadership priorities. In this context, Zhang Shengmin’s elevation to Politburo merits attention, although it does not settle the succession question.

The Fifth Plenum was primarily an exercise in reinforcing the foundations of Xi’s political system before the Party Congress. The underlying proposition is that the Party must strengthen and discipline itself to lead China’s rejuvenation. The unprecedented removal of senior functionaries, particularly within the PLA, highlights the continuing emphasis on political control.

Story continues below this ad

However, tighter political control cannot, by itself, resolve China’s economic challenges. Weak domestic consumption, property-sector stress, local government debt, demographic decline and external technology restrictions remain structural constraints. The 15th Five-Year Plan seeks to address these issues. Excessive political control can constrain private enterprise and discourage innovation. The challenge, therefore, is to balance political authority with the flexibility required for sustained economic growth.

The centrality of national security in China’s governance framework was also reinforced. Domestic governance and external policies are increasingly interconnected. Against the backdrop of intensifying US-China competition, the leadership is expected to accelerate efforts towards technological independence, military modernisation and strategic outreach.

Closer to home, China’s territorial claims and emphasis on national security will continue to shape the environment along the Line of Actual Control (LAC). The removal of senior PLA commanders should not be interpreted as a moderation of China’s strategic objectives or a dilution of its military capabilities. India must closely monitor changes in the PLA’s command structure and operational readiness while strengthening its own defence preparedness as part of a coherent China policy.

The writer is a war veteran and former Assistant Chief of Army Staff (Strategy). He has served as Defence Attaché in China and is currently a Professor at Lal Bahadur Shastri Institute of Management.

title: Jensen Huang-Alice Huang affair: How the Nvidia scandal became a US security concern
content_html:
Jensen Huang during his China visit in May 2026 (left); Alice Huang at a dinner hosted by the erstwhile Nvidia CEO at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, in May last year (AP).
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang Thursday resigned as its chief executive officer after a controversy over his extramarital affairs, two of which reportedly involved company colleagues.

But the affair that triggered his ouster was with a Chinese woman named Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le), who has been accused of passing on intelligence to China. Adding to the concerns was the fact that Huang has lobbied for easing America’s restrictions on sales of artificial intelligence (AI) chips to China in the past.

Alice Huang is a former executive from the Singapore-registered data centre operator Megaspeed, which American authorities have separately investigated since 2024 over suspicions that it was helping China access restricted AI chips.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

This is why the extramarital affair goes well beyond his personal life or his company’s future.

What’s the Jensen Huang-Alice Huang Scandal?

The Nvdia CEO’s scandal broke on October 29, when The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials were examining Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang.

Jensen Huang admitted to having the affair over the following weekend. US President Donald Trump then said the FBI was investigating the matter, but backed the Nvidia co-founder.

Nobody has been charged with any offence so far, and as per Nvidia board of director’s last statement on the matter, the company had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

Story continues below this ad

How an affair went beyond Nvidia CEO’s marriage and became a national security risk

A CEO’s private life is normally his own business. It stops being so when he is involved with a person of interest who is under surveillance by intelligence agencies. And if the CEO’s company makes the chips at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom and US-China tech race, he will be scrutinised for sure.

Also Read | Jensen Huang resigns: Why his exit from Nvidia will be a test for the AI boom

While Jensen Huang himself was not a suspect, Alice Huang and Nvidia’s deals with Megaspeed — and by extension China — have come under scrutiny.

Essentially, the concern is over how much leverage, access and influence Alice Huang had over Nvidia’s operations and decisions. Investigators reportedly wanted to know whether Chinese intelligence was using an executive relationship to learn about Nvidia’s hardware allocation, supply timelines and lobbying on export rules.

Happier Times: Jensen Huang and his wife Lori Huang walk to the White House to attend a state dinner hosted for China’s President Xi Jinping on September 24, 2026 (AP Photo)

US intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang of working for China’s Ministry of State Security, according to the Financial Times and The New York Times. Chinese state media, however, has called the claims baseless. Singapore’s Home Affairs ministry said that in February 2025, the Singapore Police Force and Singapore Customs initiated an independent investigation into several companies and their key officers, including Megaspeed International Pte Ltd, and its controllers.

Story continues below this ad

“The suspected domestic offences pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offences… Alice Huang (otherwise known as Huang Le), a Hong Kong resident, was investigated for suspected involvement in the possible offences in Singapore, given her position as then-CEO,” the Singapore government said in a statement on Thursday.

It, however, clarified that Alice Huang was not investigated for espionage.

The US House Select Committee on China called Alice Huang a “publicly reported Chinese intelligence asset” and asked her to attend a November 18 briefing.

.

HOW IT UNFOLDED
MAY 13–14Huang joins Trump’s Beijing trip as a late addition, boarding Air Force One in Alaska. Nvidia says he went at Trump’s invitation.
OCT 29NYT reports US officials believe Megaspeed’s Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset and that Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
NOV 6–7Reports (NYT, FT) on a US intelligence memo alleging China’s Ministry of State Security recruited her to spy on him.
NOV 8 · SUNNvidia’s board opens an independent investigation. Huang tells staff he “was unfaithful to my wife.”
NOV 9 · MONTrump says the FBI is looking into it, and says he believes Huang did not know she was a spy.
NOV 11 · WEDNYT, citing five people, reports a relationship with VP Kimberly Powell. The board meets that night and accepts his resignation.
NOV 12 · THUNvidia announces the resignation; Kress named interim CEO. Singapore publishes its Megaspeed findings. Reuters reports a third relationship, with another employee.
CONFIRMED · ALLEGED · DENIED
CONFIRMED
Huang resigned as CEO, president and board member; Kress is interim CEO (Nvidia).
Huang admitted to staff that he was unfaithful to his wife.
Nvidia’s board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, and opened an independent probe.
Singapore’s Home Affairs ministry says Alice Huang was not investigated for espionage.
ALLEGED (PER REPORTS)
US intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang works for China’s Ministry of State Security (NYT, FT). A House committee called her a “publicly reported” Chinese intelligence asset.
The Information reported her relationship helped steer at least $7.5bn in Nvidia sales to Chinese buyers; CNBC said it could not verify this.
NYT: a relationship with VP Kimberly Powell. Reuters: a third, with another employee. Neither has been confirmed; Nvidia declined to comment on Reuters. Reports do not allege security wrongdoing by Powell.
DENIED OR DISPUTED
China’s foreign ministry calls the spy claim unsubstantiated and “smears.”
Huang denied compromising national security or Nvidia secrets. Nvidia said his dealings with her were “not unusual” and it shares no classified information with customers.
Nvidia says it found no evidence of chip diversion and cut off Megaspeed in June 2025. Megaspeed denies illegal transfers to China.
WHY WASHINGTON IS WATCHING
The question: lawmakers want to know whether sensitive information was compromised and whether the administration responded properly (Reuters).
The access: Trump approved H200 chip sales to China in Dec 2025, with 25% of proceeds going to the US government. About 10 Chinese firms were cleared, but none had shipped by mid-May as Beijing held orders back (Reuters). Critics such as Sen. Warren say Huang lobbied for looser curbs; Nvidia says H200 sales need a US licence.
Both parties: Republicans Brian Mast and John Moolenaar want testimony; Democrats Warren and Schumer say the resignation does not end the matter.
MEGASPEED AND ALICE HUANG
MEGASPEED
Singapore-based firm that rents out computing power built on Nvidia chips; customers include Alibaba. One of Nvidia’s biggest foreign buyers (NYT, CBS).
Short-seller Culper says its balance sheet jumped from about $33m to about $3bn in 2024. The source of that money is unconfirmed.
NYT reports a US trade official saw unopened Nvidia chip boxes at a Megaspeed affiliate, raising re-export fears. Megaspeed says checks by US and Malaysian authorities and Nvidia found no violations. Renting chips in third countries is not itself barred.
ALICE HUANG (A.K.A. HUANG LE)
Former Megaspeed CEO, chair and key controller; a Hong Kong resident, per Singapore. NYT describes her as a Chinese citizen.
Singapore investigated possible false declarations on server purchases from Feb 2025. In Feb 2026 police found insufficient evidence of offences, but said she gave information she knew to be inaccurate. She got a stern warning and a re-entry ban.
WHAT TO WATCH
Huang has agreed to brief Congress before Thanksgiving (Nov 26), per Rep. Mast; the closed-door date is still being set.
Nvidia’s board is weighing internal and external candidates for a permanent CEO.
Trump and Xi are expected to meet around the APEC leaders’ meeting, Nov 18–19 (CNBC).
Allegations are attributed to the outlet or official cited and have not been tested in court. No criminal charges against Jensen Huang have been reported. Figures are as of Nov 13 and may change.
Sources: Nvidia statements and filing; NYT, Reuters, FT, Bloomberg, The Information (via CNBC, CBS, ABC, Al Jazeera, TechCrunch); Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs statement, Nov 12.
Express InfoGenIE · Explained Desk
.

Who is Alice Huang, and what is Megaspeed?

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who worked as a state-media TV reporter and then as a private banker. She was Megaspeed’s CEO, Chairperson, and one of the key controllers. She is no longer associated with the Singapore-based data centre operator with Chinese origins. Its genesis can be traced to 7Road, a Chinese gaming and cloud-computing company that US lawmakers have described as having links to the Chinese government.

Story continues below this ad

While American export controls prohibit the unauthorised shipment of certain advanced chips to China, Chinese companies can potentially obtain access to comparable computing power by renting infrastructure housed in other countries.

Also Read | Behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair lies a much bigger China controversy

Megaspeed rents out computing power from Nvidia chips housed in data centres outside China, according to Fortune. In fact, Nvidia’s biggest customer of chips in Southeast Asia was Megaspeed, a 2025 Bloomberg report said. This is why the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

According to The New York Times, Nvidia has said its checks show Megaspeed has no Chinese shareholders and that it has no evidence of chip diversion to China.

But Megaspeed’s business dealings have raised questions about the extent of its links with Chinese technology companies. According to trade records cited by The New York Times, a Malaysian affiliate of Megaspeed purchased at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia technology between June 2024 and February 2026. The company has reportedly supplied computing capacity to Alibaba and other Chinese businesses, allowing them to access Nvidia-powered infrastructure located outside China.

Story continues below this ad

Megaspeed’s Southeast Asia footprint

The company grew fast. South China Morning Post, citing Singapore corporate records, reports that Megaspeed’s assets jumped roughly 90-fold from late 2023 to 2024, to almost $3 billion. Revenue went from nothing in 2023 to more than $294 million in 2024.

Bloomberg reported that Megaspeed rents out Nvidia chips at several Southeast Asian facilities to Alibaba. Its data centres are in Malaysia and Indonesia. This setup is what Washington is worried about. Chinese firms can use computing power in Singapore and Malaysia without importing the restricted chips themselves, according to a experts quoted by Fortune and Forbes. Such arrangements may be legal if the operator isn’t acting on behalf of a Chinese entity.

 

The timeline raises questions. Alice Huang was photographed with Jensen Huang at Taiwan events in 2024 and 2025. Megaspeed was placing huge orders during the same period. The Information reported that she used her relationship with him to help Megaspeed secure $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chip sales for China.

A US Commerce Department investigation in late 2024 reportedly reportedly found unopened boxes of brand new Nvidia chips at a facility operated by Speedmatrix, a subsidiary of Megaspeed. This gave rise to suspicions of the chips being smuggled to China. According to CNBC, Speedmatrix was substantially funded in “secret” by Chinese ecommerce giant Alibaba through “shell companies”.

Story continues below this ad

After the 2024, Megaspeed paused direct orders, but Speedmatrix continued to acquire Nvidia chips. According to New York Times, between 2024 and February 2026, Speedmatrix acquired at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment, Nvidia chips-enabled systems.

Huang’s Beijing visit with Donald Trump

Jensen Huang had immense access to Trump, serving on the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and accompanying him on high-level diplomatic trips, including a May 2026 visit to Beijing. As head of Nvidia and a presidential advisor, Huang had deep insight into next-generation semiconductor roadmaps, US’s own supply chain vulnerabilities, and high-level government deliberations regarding AI competition with China.

Counterintelligence experts raised alarms over exactly over this and flagged concerns regarding what sensitive information Alice might have procured during her relationship with Jensen.

Jensen Huang and Donald Trump during a White House event in September 2026 (AP Photo)

Huang reportedly lobbied fiercely with the administration to take a lighter regulatory approach to AI and successfully pushed for approvals to sell advanced chips to China. Officials feared foreign intelligence could have used the relationship to indirectly shape US trade and technology policy.

Story continues below this ad

Huang’s trip to Beijing with Trump wasn’t on the original itinerary. Trump called and invited him, and he joined the plane in Alaska. Nvidia said he attended at Trump’s invitation.

The big prize was already in hand. Trump approved H200 chip exports to China in December, and formal licences followed. Just before the summit, Reuters reported that the US had cleared about 10 Chinese firms, including Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance and JD.com, to buy H200s. The Beijing trip itself delivered little. The Reuters report stated that no H200 chips had been delivered at that point because Beijing was holding back.

With Nvidia chips being used in global AI technologies as well as US military equipment, Chinese extortion or coercion, too, remains a major worry. 

The Kimberly Powell report

On November 11, The New York Times again reported that Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare, who reported to him. In the report, NYT cited five people who had worked at the company. Reuters on Thursday reported a third affair by Jensen, again with a company executive.

Story continues below this ad

Nvidia is yet to comment on the allegations. Powell has not been accused of any security wrongdoing, and the board’s announced investigation does not mention her.

NYT reports US officials believe Megaspeed’s Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset and that Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Reports (NYT, FT) on a US intelligence memo alleging China’s Ministry of State Security recruited her to spy on him.
NOV 8 · SUN
Nvidia’s board opens an independent investigation. Huang tells staff he “was unfaithful to my wife.”
NOV 9 · MON
Trump says the FBI is looking into it, and says he believes Huang did not know she was a spy.
NOV 11 · WED
NYT, citing five people, reports a relationship with VP Kimberly Powell. The board meets that night and accepts his resignation.
NOV 12 · THU
Nvidia announces the resignation; Kress named interim CEO. Singapore publishes its Megaspeed findings. Reuters reports a third relationship, with another employee.
CONFIRMED · ALLEGED · DENIED
CONFIRMED
Huang resigned as CEO, president and board member; Kress is interim CEO (Nvidia).
Huang admitted to staff that he was unfaithful to his wife.
Nvidia’s board said it had
no reason to believe
national security or company secrets were compromised, and opened an independent probe.
Singapore’s Home Affairs ministry says Alice Huang was
not investigated for espionage
.
ALLEGED (PER REPORTS)
US intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang works for China’s Ministry of State Security (NYT, FT). A House committee called her a “publicly reported” Chinese intelligence asset.
The Information reported her relationship helped steer at least
$7.5bn
in Nvidia sales to Chinese buyers; CNBC said it could not verify this.
NYT: a relationship with VP Kimberly Powell. Reuters: a third, with another employee. Neither has been confirmed; Nvidia declined to comment on Reuters. Reports do not allege security wrongdoing by Powell.
DENIED OR DISPUTED
China’s foreign ministry calls the spy claim unsubstantiated and “smears.”
Huang denied compromising national security or Nvidia secrets. Nvidia said his dealings with her were “not unusual” and it shares no classified information with customers.
Nvidia says it found no evidence of chip diversion and cut off Megaspeed in June 2025. Megaspeed denies illegal transfers to China.

The question:
lawmakers want to know whether sensitive information was compromised and whether the administration responded properly (Reuters).
The access:
Trump approved H200 chip sales to China in Dec 2025, with 25% of proceeds going to the US government. About 10 Chinese firms were cleared, but none had shipped by mid-May as Beijing held orders back (Reuters). Critics such as Sen. Warren say Huang lobbied for looser curbs; Nvidia says H200 sales need a US licence.
Both parties:
Republicans Brian Mast and John Moolenaar want testimony; Democrats Warren and Schumer say the resignation does not end the matter.

MEGASPEED
Singapore-based firm that rents out computing power built on Nvidia chips; customers include Alibaba. One of Nvidia’s biggest foreign buyers (NYT, CBS).
Short-seller Culper says its balance sheet jumped from about $33m to about $3bn in 2024. The source of that money is unconfirmed.
