Former Megaspeed CEO, chair and key controller; a Hong Kong resident, per Singapore. NYT describes her as a Chinese citizen.
Singapore investigated possible false declarations on server purchases from Feb 2025. In Feb 2026 police found insufficient evidence of offences, but said she gave information she knew to be inaccurate. She got a stern warning and a re-entry ban.
WHAT TO WATCH
Huang has agreed to brief Congress before Thanksgiving (Nov 26), per Rep. Mast; the closed-door date is still being set.
Nvidia’s board is weighing internal and external candidates for a permanent CEO.
Trump and Xi are expected to meet around the APEC leaders’ meeting, Nov 18–19 (CNBC).
Allegations are attributed to the outlet or official cited and have not been tested in court. No criminal charges against Jensen Huang have been reported. Figures are as of Nov 13 and may change.

.
Who is Alice Huang, and what is Megaspeed?
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who worked as a state-media TV reporter and then as a private banker. She was Megaspeed’s CEO, Chairperson, and one of the key controllers. She is no longer associated with the Singapore-based data centre operator with Chinese origins. Its genesis can be traced to 7Road, a Chinese gaming and cloud-computing company that US lawmakers have described as having links to the Chinese government.
Story continues below this ad
While American export controls prohibit the unauthorised shipment of certain advanced chips to China, Chinese companies can potentially obtain access to comparable computing power by renting infrastructure housed in other countries.
Also Read
|

Megaspeed rents out computing power from Nvidia chips housed in data centres outside China, according to
Fortune
. In fact, Nvidia’s biggest customer of chips in Southeast Asia was Megaspeed, a 2025
Bloomberg
report said. This is why the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.
According to
The New York Times
, Nvidia has said its checks show Megaspeed has no Chinese shareholders and that it has no evidence of chip diversion to China.

The New York Times
, a Malaysian affiliate of Megaspeed purchased at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia technology between June 2024 and February 2026. Story continues below this ad
Megaspeed’s Southeast Asia footprint
The company grew fast.
South China Morning Post

Bloomberg
reported that Megaspeed rents out Nvidia chips at several Southeast Asian facilities to Alibaba. Its data centres are in Malaysia and Indonesia. This setup is what Washington is worried about. Chinese firms can use computing power in Singapore and Malaysia without importing the restricted chips themselves, according to a experts quoted by
Fortune
and
Forbes
. Such arrangements may be legal if the operator isn’t acting on behalf of a Chinese entity.
The timeline raises questions.
Alice Huang was photographed with Jensen Huang
at Taiwan events in 2024 and 2025. Megaspeed was placing huge orders during the same period.
The Information
reported that she used her relationship with him to help Megaspeed secure $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chip sales for China.
A US Commerce Department investigation in late 2024 reportedly reportedly found unopened boxes of brand new Nvidia chips at a facility operated by Speedmatrix, a subsidiary of Megaspeed. Story continues below this ad
After the 2024, Megaspeed paused direct orders, but Speedmatrix continued to acquire Nvidia chips. According to
New York Times

NYT

title: Blue Flag beaches: What it takes to earn this global tag, held by just 22 in India
content_html:
Shrivardhan beach in Maharashtra's Raigad district. (Wikimedia Commons)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

In a first for Maharashtra, three of its beaches have been awarded an international certification that recognises beaches meeting stringent standards of environmental protection, water quality, safety and tourist facilities.

The Ladghar and Guhagar beaches in Ratnagiri district, and the Shrivardhan beach in Raigad district, have earned the international Blue Flag certification. Only 22 beaches in India carry the certification, awarded by a Denmark-based non-governmental organisation. What does it take to earn the tag, and what do its standards entail?

 What is the Blue Flag tag?

The Blue Flag is an internationally recognised voluntary eco-label awarded to beaches, marinas and tourism boats that meet prescribed standards of environmental management, water quality, safety, accessibility and environmental education.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The programme is run by the Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE), an international non-governmental, non-profit organisation headquartered in Copenhagen, Denmark. It began in France in 1985 and has since grown into a global certification programme.

Also Read | 7 Blue Flag beaches in India worth exploring

Unlike awards that recognise a destination’s popularity or tourism potential, the Blue Flag assesses how a beach is managed. The emphasis is on whether its bathing water is safe, waste is disposed of responsibly, the surrounding ecosystem is protected and visitors have access to basic safety and other facilities.

Who decides which beaches get the Blue Flag?

The certification process is overseen by the FEE, which works through national operators in participating countries. Applications are first examined at the national level before being sent to the International Blue Flag Jury for a final decision.

Story continues below this ad

The international jury includes representatives of organisations and experts working in environmental protection, tourism, water quality, coastal management and accessibility. These include the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), UNESCO, UN Tourism and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

Guhagar beaches in Ratnagiri district. (Wikimedia Commons)

In India, a National Blue Flag Jury comprising experts, government representatives and members of civil society examines applications and recommends beaches for international consideration. The final decision rests with the FEE’s International Jury.

What does a beach have to do to qualify for a Blue Flag tag?

India’s Blue Flag programme prescribes 33 criteria, grouped under four broad heads: environmental education and information, water quality, environmental management, and safety and services.

Environmental education and information: Beaches must display information about the local ecosystem, bathing water quality, available facilities and appropriate visitor conduct. They are also required to organise activities to raise awareness about the coastal environment.

Story continues below this ad

Water quality: This is among the most critical requirements. Beaches must undergo regular water sampling and testing and meet prescribed standards for microbiological contamination, including E. coli and intestinal enterococci. Sewage, industrial waste and other discharges must not contaminate bathing waters.

Ladghar beach in Ratnagiri district. (Wikimedia Commons)

Environmental management: Authorities must ensure regular cleaning, proper waste collection and segregation, and adequate sewage disposal. They must also protect sensitive habitats and local biodiversity. Tourism infrastructure and other activities should not come at the cost of the surrounding ecosystem.

Safety and services: Beaches must have first aid facilities and emergency arrangements, along with appropriate public safety measures. Basic visitor amenities include drinking water and toilets. Accessibility for persons with disabilities is also part of the assessment.

Does a beach get to keep the tag permanently?

No. The Blue Flag is awarded for a particular season and has to be renewed. Beaches must continue to meet the prescribed criteria throughout the certification period.

Story continues below this ad

National operators carry out monitoring and control visits, while the international programme also provides for inspections. If a beach fails to maintain the required standards, authorities can be asked to take corrective measures. The certification can also be suspended or withdrawn.

How many beaches worldwide and in India have the Blue Flag tag?

According to the FEE’s announcement for the 2026 Northern Hemisphere season, 5,274 sites across 53 countries had received Blue Flag recognition. These included 4,371 beaches, 745 marinas and 158 tourism boats.

In India, 22 beaches have received the certification for the 2026 to 2027 season. Of these, 13 are renewals and nine are new additions. The three Maharashtra beaches are among the new entrants.

Story continues below this ad

India’s first eight beaches received the Blue Flag certification in 2020. Since then, the programme has expanded to cover more coastal destinations across the country.

What does the recognition mean for Maharashtra?

Ladghar, Guhagar and Shrivardhan are the first beaches in Maharashtra to make it to the Blue Flag list. Their inclusion gives the state’s coastline international recognition for environmental management and sustainable tourism.

The state government intends to use the programme to bring more eligible beaches along the Maharashtra coast up to international standards. The certification could also improve the visibility of these destinations among tourists and provide a boost to local tourism related businesses.

title: How does Parliament convene special sessions, and what sets them apart?
content_html:
The power to convene a session of Parliament rests with the government. (File)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The Indian Express reported on Friday (November 13) that a special session of Parliament could be convened before the regularly scheduled Winter Session this year. The Centre is planning to do so to secure passage of its legislative agenda on delimitation of electoral constituencies and implementation of women’s reservation.

Sources said this could be the last window to advance the implementation of women’s quota to 2029, when the Lok Sabha elections are scheduled to be held.

In the ordinary course, Parliament holds three sessions: the Budget Session, Monsoon Session and the Winter Session. Here are the provisions that govern them, and what entails a special session.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Sessions of Indian Parliament

The power to convene a session of Parliament rests with the government. The decision is taken by the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs, which currently comprises 10 ministers, including those for Defence, Home and Finance. The committee’s decision is formalised by the President, in whose name MPs are summoned to meet for a session.

India does not have a fixed parliamentary calendar. The Constitution specifies that six months should not elapse between two parliamentary sessions. The framers of the Constitution borrowed it from the Government of India Act of 1935.

By convention, Parliament meets for three sessions in a year. The longest, the Budget Session, starts towards the end of January and concludes by the end of April or the first week of May. The session has a recess so that Parliamentary Committees can discuss the budgetary proposals.

Research | The historical journey of parliamentary sessions in India

The second session is the three-week Monsoon Session, which usually begins in July and finishes in August. The parliamentary year ends with a three-week-long Winter Session, which is held from November to December. This Winter Session is expected to begin in late November or early December.

Story continues below this ad

Notably, as of November 12 this year, the Monsoon Session of Parliament has not been prorogued for 91 days since being adjourned sine die (postponed without a new day for reconvening) on August 13. This is the longest such adjournment in history, and it means Parliament can be convened any day without the mandatory 14-day notice required before the House is called into session, government sources said.

What the Constitution says on Parliament sessions

The summoning of Parliament is specified in Article 85 of the Constitution. Like many other Articles, it is based on a provision of the Government of India Act, 1935. This provision specified that the central legislature had to be summoned to meet at least once a year, and that not more than 12 months could elapse between two sessions.

Dr B R Ambedkar’s drafting of the provision reduced the gap between sessions to six months, and specified that Parliament should meet at least twice a year. He argued that “The clause as it stands does not prevent the legislature from being summoned more often than what has been provided for in the clause itself. In fact, my fear is, if I may say so, that the sessions of Parliament would be so frequent and so lengthy that the members of the legislature would probably themselves get tired of the sessions.”

Over the years, governments have shuffled around the dates of sessions to accommodate political and legislative exigencies. In 2017, the Winter Session was delayed on account of the Gujarat Assembly elections. In 2011, political parties agreed to cut short the Budget Session so they could campaign for Legislative Assembly elections in five states.

Story continues below this ad

Sessions have also been cut short or delayed to allow the government to issue Ordinances. For example, in 2016, the Budget Session was broken up into two separate sessions to enable the issuance of an Ordinance.

Special session of Parliament

The Constitution does not use the term “special session”. The term sometimes refers to sessions the government has convened for specific occasions, like commemorating parliamentary or national milestones.

For the two Houses to be in session, the presiding officers (the Lok Sabha Speaker and Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) should chair their proceedings. The presiding officers can also direct that the proceedings of their respective Houses be limited, and procedural devices like Question Hour would not be available to MPs during the session.

While Article 85 empowers the President to summon Parliament, the convention is to give around 15 days’ notice for a regular session. A special session, however, can be convened at shorter notice. If a session has been adjourned sine die but not prorogued (meaning formally ending a session), it technically remains alive, and the Lok Sabha can be reconvened at short notice by the Speaker under Rule 15 of the Rules of Procedure.

Story continues below this ad

However, Article 352 (Proclamation of Emergency) of the Constitution does refer to a “special sitting of the House”. Parliament added the part relating to the special sitting through the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978. Its purpose was to add safeguards to the power of proclaiming an Emergency in the country, after the events of 1975 under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. It specifies that if a Proclamation of Emergency is issued and Parliament is not in session, then one-tenth of Lok Sabha MPs can ask the President to convene a special meeting to disapprove the Emergency.

This explainer uses information from earlier articles (published in 2020 and 2023) written by Chakshu Roy, Head of Outreach at PRS Legislative Research.
